content: A micelle is a structure formed by the aggregation of surfactant molecules in a liquid colloid. In an aqueous solution, micelles typically consist of surfactant molecules arranged such that their hydrophilic head groups are in contact with the surrounding water, while their hydrophobic tail groups are sequestered in the interior of the micelle. This arrangement is referred to as a normal phase micelle or an oil-in-water micelle. Conversely, in inverse micelles, the hydrophilic head groups are located at the center, and the hydrophobic tails extend outward, forming a water-in-oil micelle. Micelles are generally spherical in shape, but other configurations, such as ellipsoids, cylinders, and bilayers, can also occur depending on the molecular geometry of the surfactant and the conditions of the solution, including surfactant concentration, temperature, pH, and ionic strength. The process by which micelles form is called micellization, and it is a key aspect of the phase behavior of many lipids, influenced by their polymorphic properties. The concept of micelles has a historical foundation. While the detergent properties of soapy solutions have been recognized for centuries, the scientific study of their constitution began in the early 20th century. James William McBain, a researcher at the University of Bristol, proposed the existence of colloidal ions in 1913 to explain the high electrolytic conductivity of sodium palmitate solutions. These spontaneously formed, highly mobile clusters were later termed micelles, a term popularized by G.S. Hartley in his seminal work, Paraffin Chain Salts, A Study in Micelle Formation. In a solution, surfactant molecules that are not part of a micelle are referred to as monomers. In water, the hydrophilic head groups of surfactant molecules are always in contact with the solvent, whether the molecules exist as monomers or as part of a micelle. However, the hydrophobic tails of surfactant molecules are less exposed to water when they are incorporated into a micelle. Within a micelle, the hydrophobic tails cluster together to form an oil-like core, which is stabilized by minimizing contact with water. In contrast, surfactant monomers are surrounded by water molecules that form a structured cage through hydrogen bonding, resembling a clathrate with an ice-like crystalline structure. Micelles formed from ionic surfactants exhibit electrostatic interactions with surrounding counterions in the solution. These counterions partially neutralize the charge of the micelle, masking up to 90% of its surface charge. However, the residual charge of the micelle can still influence the structure of the surrounding solvent over significant distances. The presence of ionic micelles affects various properties of the solution, including its electrical conductivity. Adding salts to a colloidal solution containing micelles can reduce the strength of electrostatic interactions, leading to the formation of larger ionic micelles. This phenomenon can be understood in terms of changes in the hydration state of the system. Micelle formation occurs only when the concentration of surfactant exceeds the critical micelle concentration (CMC) and the temperature of the system is above the critical micelle temperature, also known as the Krafft temperature. The thermodynamics of micelle formation involve a balance between entropy and enthalpy. In aqueous systems, the hydrophobic effect drives micelle formation, even though the aggregation of surfactant molecules reduces their entropy. Above the CMC, the entropic cost of assembling surfactant molecules is outweighed by the entropic penalty of water molecules forming structured cages around individual surfactant monomers. Enthalpic factors, such as electrostatic interactions between charged surfactant groups, also play a significant role in micelle formation. In this case, the hydrophilic groups are sequestered in the micelle core, while the hydrophobic tails extend outward. The likelihood of forming inverse micelles decreases with increasing charge on the head groups, as this would result in highly unfavorable electrostatic interactions within the micelle core. Micelles have numerous practical applications. When surfactants are present above the CMC, they act as emulsifiers, enabling the dissolution of compounds that are otherwise insoluble in the solvent. This occurs because the insoluble species can be incorporated into the micelle core, which is stabilized in the bulk solvent by the favorable interactions of the head groups with the solvent. A common example of this phenomenon is the use of detergents, which clean lipophilic substances such as oils and waxes that cannot be removed by water alone. Detergents also reduce the surface tension of water, facilitating the removal of materials from surfaces. The emulsifying properties of surfactants are also critical in processes such as emulsion polymerization. In biological systems, micelle formation is essential for the absorption of fat-soluble vitamins and complex lipids. Bile salts, produced in the liver and secreted by the gallbladder, facilitate the formation of micelles containing fatty acids. These micelles enable the absorption of complex lipids, such as lecithin, and lipid-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, and K) in the small intestine.
